It is doing real rhetorical work — it is the sentence that turns a 3 pp effect into "modest but important" — so it should be traceable and is not.

SELF-CONTAINMENT OF EXHIBITS

The four estimation tables are mostly well built. Each note specifies the estimator (local linear, triangular kernel), the bandwidth selector (Calonico et al. 2014), the clustering (eighth-grade school), that Columns 2 and 4 add student, school, and region covariates, and what "Control" means. Control means are printed for every row — genuinely useful, since almost all outcomes are binary and the raw coefficients are meaningless without a base. Table 5's note defines "on-time" and "college-ready" precisely enough to reproduce.

The gaps: (1) The bandwidth in the notes (5.36, and 5.25 for Table 3) contradicts the methods text's "5 points ... for all of our main results," and the Table 3 discrepancy is never explained. (2) Table 3's note says "For this analysis, we exclude students who did not take the Algebra I EOC before ninth grade" — "before ninth grade" is confusing on its face, and "this analysis" is ambiguous across a table covering five exams with ten different Ns. (3) Table 1 gives percentages with no SDs, no N per variable, and two unlabeled "Observations" blocks (208,060/21,044 and 184,274/20,635), with no note explaining the second. (4) Table 1's note defines the analytic sample differently from the Sample section — adding a "without receiving linguistic accommodations" exclusion that appears nowhere in the text, and a ±2 SD window the text never mentions. (5) The "CATE" acronym is expanded as "complier average treatment effect" in the text (p. 10) and "complier local average treatment effect" in every table note.

Figure 1 is the only figure. It shows binned means with fitted lines on either side of the cutoff and a clear jump, but it has no confidence band, no SE on the stated 39-point difference, no statement of bandwidth or bin width, and no N; its note also carries a stray doubled period. The visual jump between the two fitted lines at zero looks somewhat larger than 39 points, which a careful reader will notice and be unable to reconcile from the figure alone.

The deeper exposition problem is that no outcome is ever plotted. In an RD paper, outcome plots are how readers independently judge whether a discontinuity exists and whether functional form is doing the work. Here the reader must accept coefficient tables on faith. Combined with the offloading of all 35 appendix tables and both appendix figures to the online supplement — including every balance, manipulation, falsification, attrition, bandwidth, and mechanism exhibit — the printed article asks for considerably more trust than it lets the reader verify. The mechanism argument on pp. 18–19 is the sharpest case: the paper's explanation for its own alarming negative results (that reclassifiers lose ESL supports in non-ELA content courses) is delivered entirely as prose point estimates with no exhibit and explicit acknowledgment that they are imprecise.

ABSTRACT

Ninety-eight words, and the two sentences of findings are directionally faithful but stripped of scope. "Reclassified students earn more advanced credits, but graduate high school at lower rates" is true of Tables 2 and 5. What is missing is who these students are and what they are being compared to. The population is eighth-grade Texas ML-ELs who had already met all three TELPAS "advanced high" domains and who failed STAAR Reading on the first attempt — 21,044 of 208,060 (Table 1), with estimation samples nearer 12,000. And the comparison group receives accelerated instruction, which the authors themselves identify as the crux: "the counterfactual to reclassification in our study is remaining EL and accessing additional academic support" (p. 2). Neither appears in the abstract. The abstract also flattens the course-taking result — the gains are in English and social studies, with precise nulls in math and science — and gives no magnitudes, so "graduate high school at lower rates" will be read as far larger than a 2.2 pp ITT off a 90.5% base. The policy inference ("indicating a need for greater course access ... and increased support for former ML-ELs") is stated without hedging, though the body is appropriately cautious ("Our mixed results do not offer conclusive evidence on how states should incorporate academic criteria," p. 2). Finally, the title's either/or framing ("Bulwark or Barrier?") is answered "both" — resolved explicitly on p. 17, but a reader who sees only the title and abstract may expect a verdict the paper does not deliver.

DENSITY AND WHAT TO SKIP

The Conceptual Framework (pp. 2–5) is roughly a fifth of the article and is a conventional review; specialists lose nothing by skimming it. The three "Implications" subsections (pp. 19–21) are standard recommendations (recruit MLs into AP, remove teacher-recommendation gates, fund exam vouchers, study LPAC accommodation decisions) that are only loosely tied to this paper's estimates. What must not be skipped: the State Policy Context (pp. 5–6), because the ELA-for-ELP substitution and the relative pass rates invert the intuitive reading of the design; the Sample section (p. 7), because the second-administration restriction defines the population and creates the accelerated-instruction counterfactual; the exclusion-restriction paragraph (p. 11) and footnote 6 (p. 22), which together concede that the control group may be receiving extra reading support — the single largest threat to interpreting the negative results as an effect of reclassification rather than of support loss; and Generalizability and Limitations (pp. 19–20), which is candid and well written and states plainly that the results do not speak to the current Texas policy of requiring both ELA and ELP.

OVERALL

The exposition is clearly above average for the genre: organized, signposted, honest about uncertainty in most places, and unusually attentive to anticipating reader objections. It falls short of strong because the errors that survived production are not cosmetic — one of them reverses the meaning of a headline estimate in plain language, and another makes the significance markings in the graduation table internally contradictory — and because the abstract, which is what most readers will actually consume, omits precisely the restrictions the authors elsewhere insist on.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Strong (moderate confidence)

Xu, Flanagan, and Quintero deliver the first statewide, large-N causal evidence on eighth-grade EL reclassification in Texas, using a frontier RD that conditions on meeting all TELPAS oral/writing thresholds and then exploits the STAAR Reading cutoff — an unusually clean way to isolate the marginal contribution of an academic content criterion rather than a binding-score composite. The headline result is genuinely mixed: reclassification raises advanced course credit (ITT +3.1 pp on a 10.1% base; CATE +7.5 pp, p. 13) but lowers on-time graduation (ITT −4.1 pp on an 83.3% base; CATE −10.1 pp, p. 16). The course-access finding is the most novel and best-supported contribution; the negative achievement/graduation cluster is real but travels less far than the title and abstract suggest, because the below-cutoff counterfactual bundles continued EL status with state-mandated accelerated reading instruction, and because Texas during the study period used ELA as a substitute for an ELP reading test, not as an added criterion.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely new causal evidence on advanced coursework. Three prior RD studies (Reyes & Hwang 2021; Robinson 2011; Umansky 2016b) found no effect of EL classification on advanced course engagement (p. 5). This paper finds a positive, precisely estimated reclassification effect concentrated in the humanities — advanced English ITT +2.2 pp / CATE +5.4 pp on a 4.2% base, advanced social studies ITT +2.6 pp / CATE +6.2 pp on a 6.9% base (Table 2, p. 13). That effectively doubles the base rate for compliers and converts a large descriptive literature on EL tracking (Callahan 2005; Callahan et al. 2010; Kanno & Kangas 2014) into a causal claim. This is the paper's clearest standalone addition.
- The frontier/multiple-rating RD design is the right instrument for the stated question and is under-used in this literature. By first restricting to students who scored "advanced high" on TELPAS speaking, listening, and writing (32% of eighth-grade ML-ELs, p. 7) and only then using the STAAR cutoff, the authors sidestep the standard binding-score collapse that the paper correctly criticizes (p. 4). Very few reclassification studies can say which criterion is doing the work; this one can.
- Setting and scale. Texas serves the highest share of EL-classified students of any state (~20% of enrollment, p. 5) and had gone essentially unstudied with credible designs; the prior literature is dominated by single California districts, especially LAUSD (p. 5). Statewide administrative data across five cohorts, 21,044 students in the 2-SD sample and ~11,000–13,000 within the 5.36-point optimal bandwidth, gives this far more power and coverage than the typical district RD.
- The eighth-grade / middle-to-high-school transition timing is well-motivated and thinly evidenced elsewhere. Effects that operate through ninth-grade course placement plausibly compound across four years, and the paper's own advanced-credit results (courses typically taken in Grades 11–12) support that reading (p. 17).
- Design credibility work is thorough and reported: covariate smoothness (Table A4), density/manipulation tests that fail to reject smoothness in any year (Table A5), a 39-percentage-point first stage (Figure 1, p. 11), donut/threshold-shift falsification at ±4 points that returns uniformly null point estimates, bandwidths from 4 to 10 points, COVID-cohort exclusion, and three separate attrition checks (p. 17). The paper also discloses the one place robustness bites: conditioning on students with all outcomes non-missing kills significance on the Algebra I score effect (p. 17).
- The Generalizability and Limitations section (p. 19) is unusually candid for this literature. It names the substitute-vs-additional-criterion problem, names the low STAAR threshold relative to TELPAS, and explicitly declines to claim the results speak to the current Texas/California/New York/Florida regime that requires both ELA and ELP.
- Honest handling of an awkward internal tension. Footnote 7 (p. 22) confronts head-on the oddity that reclassifiers both earn more advanced English/social studies credit and fail more courses in those same subjects, and offers a checkable decomposition (about 70% of advanced-course takers never fail a core humanities course).

**Weaknesses:**

- The estimand does not match the framing question, and this is the paper's central citation hazard. The title, abstract, and "Reassessing the Use of Academic Content Criteria" section (pp. 19–20) all pose the question as whether states should use academic criteria in reclassification. But Texas during 2013–2017 used STAAR ELA in place of an ELP reading test (pp. 5–6), so the comparison is not "ELA criterion added vs. not added" — it is "a relatively lenient ELA reading bar vs. no reading bar at all." Eighteen states include non-ELP assessments, and the four largest ML-EL states now stack ELA on top of ELP (p. 2) — precisely the configuration this design cannot evaluate. The authors say so on p. 19; readers who stop at the abstract will not.
- The exclusion restriction is compromised in a way that directly loads on the negative results. Failing STAAR triggers state-mandated accelerated instruction (footnote 6, p. 22), so the control condition is "stayed EL and received extra reading support," as the authors concede on p. 2 ("the counterfactual to reclassification in our study is remaining EL and accessing additional academic support"). The paper also acknowledges STAAR passage may shape ninth-grade course placement (p. 11). Every negative estimate — Algebra I EOC −0.13 SD CATE, +10.7 pp core English failure, −10.1 pp on-time graduation — is therefore a compound of losing EL services, losing accelerated instruction, and possible tracking effects, and none of the three is separately identified. There is no attempt to bound or probe this (e.g., districts with weak vs. strong accelerated-instruction implementation, which footnote 6 says varies widely).
- The reclassification-effects half of the paper is closer to replication than to new knowledge. "Lenient exit criteria produce negative high school outcomes" is the LAUSD finding from Robinson-Cimpian & Thompson (2016) and Betts et al. (2020), including the detail that the harm disappears once criteria tighten (pp. 3–4). Texas subsequently added the ELP reading exam (p. 20), so the specific policy configuration studied here no longer exists in the state. That does not make the evidence uninformative, but it means the contribution is "confirms the LAUSD pattern at statewide scale in a decentralized, high-stakes-testing state" rather than "overturns prior belief."
- The graduation magnitudes strain the causal story relative to their identification. A 10-percentage-point CATE decline in on-time graduation off an 83.3% base — and a 5.4 pp CATE increase in dropout off a 9.5% base — from a marginal-score label change is very large by the standards of this literature, and the paper reports that estimates generally grow as bandwidth shrinks (p. 17), a pattern that can indicate noise as easily as bias reduction. Combined with the accelerated-instruction confound, the honest reading is that this magnitude is an upper bound on any reclassification-only effect.
- Roughly 25 outcomes are tested (3 advanced-credit aggregates + 4 subject-specific + 2 remedial + 5 EOC scores + 5 retakes + 4 course-failure + 4 graduation) with no multiplicity correction. Several results the discussion leans on are marginal: Algebra I retake is significant only at p < .1 in the preferred specification (Table 3, pp. 14–15), and social studies course failure is p < .1 (Table 4, p. 15). The graduation cluster is the robust one; the achievement cluster is thinner than the discussion's language ("which is alarming," p. 17) implies.
- Mechanism evidence is explicitly weak but is doing real interpretive work. The ESL-All-Content vs. ESL-ELA-Only split yields a −0.2 SD Algebra I estimate the authors themselves flag as "not significant at conventional levels," and the school-EL-share split is described as imprecise due to small samples (p. 18). Yet the discussion's summary claim — "negative effects of reclassification seem to be most pronounced in schools with more comprehensive EL services and larger populations of ML-ELs" (p. 19) — reads as more established than the underlying appendix estimates support, and the paper concedes the ESL-All-Content pattern is equally consistent with two opposite mechanisms.
- The sample is doubly selected in ways that limit reach: students must have met all three TELPAS domains (32% of eighth-grade ML-ELs) and have failed the first STAAR administration and retaken it. Ninety-five percent have been in U.S. schools 5+ years and seventh-grade achievement is well below the ML-EL average (Table 1, p. 8). The authors argue this long-term-ML-EL, high-oral/low-academic-literacy profile is policy-relevant and common (p. 19) — a fair argument — but it is a specific and unusual population, not "ML-ELs at the reclassification margin" generally.
- The abstract's policy conclusion picks one of two equally supported readings without saying so. "Increased support for former ML-ELs" is a plausible inference from post-exit struggle, but the same evidence supports "the exit bar was set too low" — the conclusion Texas itself drew by adding the ELP reading requirement. The paper acknowledges the ambiguity on p. 20 ("difficult to disentangle whether the negative effects ... are driven by the content assessed on the ELA exam or by the lower passing standard"), but the abstract does not.
- Longer-run outcomes stop at high school graduation (through spring 2022). Given that the positive finding is about AP/IB/DE credit — whose value is largely postsecondary — the paper cannot tell readers whether the course-access gain converts into college enrollment or credit accumulation, which is where Carlson & Knowles (2016) found their strongest effects.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the first credible causal evidence that EL classification itself constrains access to advanced coursework. The advanced-credit results (Table 2, p. 13) are the paper's best-identified, most novel finding, they are stable to covariates and bandwidth, and they meaningfully update three prior null RD studies. This is now the reference for "EL status is a barrier to AP/IB/DE participation, not merely correlated with lower participation."
- CITE IT FOR: statewide RD evidence on eighth-grade reclassification in Texas. It is the best available evidence for that state and grade, and it usefully breaks the field's dependence on single California districts. Pair it with Carlson & Knowles (2016, Wisconsin), Cimpian et al. (2017), and Johnson (2019) when characterizing how context-dependent secondary reclassification effects are.
- CITE IT FOR: the specific claim that a low-threshold, ELA-only reading criterion permits exit before students are academically ready, for high-ELP / low-academic-literacy long-term ML-ELs. State the population and the threshold when you cite it — the finding is about a lenient bar, not about academic criteria as a category.
- CITE IT FOR: methodological demonstration that a frontier/multiple-rating RD can isolate which reclassification criterion binds, instead of collapsing criteria into a binding score. This is a transferable design template for the 18 states with multi-criterion exit rules.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: "academic criteria in reclassification are harmful" or "states should drop ELA requirements." The design evaluates ELA substituting for ELP reading at a relatively low bar; it cannot speak to the modal current policy — including present-day Texas, California, New York, and Florida — where ELA is layered on top of full ELP requirements (paper's own caveat, p. 19).
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: "reclassification reduces high school graduation" as a clean causal fact. The below-cutoff comparison group received state-mandated accelerated reading instruction (p. 2; footnote 6, p. 22), so the estimate bundles losing EL services with losing an academic intervention. Treat −4.1 pp ITT / −10.1 pp CATE on on-time graduation as an upper bound on any reclassification-only effect.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: average effects of reclassification on ML-ELs. The sample is ML-ELs who met all three TELPAS domains and failed the first STAAR and retook it — 95% with 5+ years in U.S. schools, with below-average seventh-grade achievement (Table 1, p. 8). It is a long-term-ML-EL margin, not a general one.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: mechanisms. The ESL-All-Content vs. ELA-Only and high- vs. low-EL-share school splits (p. 18) are underpowered and, by the authors' own reading, consistent with opposite explanations. If you need the "losing EL services drives the harm" claim, cite it as the authors' hypothesis, not as their finding.
- READ THE MOST-QUOTABLE-VS-BEST-SUPPORTED GAP DELIBERATELY. The title's "bulwark or barrier" and the abstract's "earn more advanced credits, but graduate high school at lower rates" will be the quoted line. The advanced-credit half is the better-identified half; the graduation half carries the confound. Expect the paper to be cited primarily for the half it supports less firmly.
- OPEN QUESTIONS A READER SHOULD KNOW REMAIN: (1) whether requiring ELA in addition to ELP — the policy actually in force in the largest ML-EL states — helps or harms, which this design cannot answer and the authors flag as the priority for follow-on work (p. 20); (2) whether the effect is about test content (higher-order reading) or threshold height, which Texas's configuration confounds; (3) whether the advanced-credit gain converts into postsecondary enrollment or credits, given the data stop at graduation; (4) whether the graduation effect survives separating loss of EL services from loss of accelerated instruction; (5) whether the same subgroups drive both the advanced-credit gain and the course-failure increase, which footnote 7 (p. 22) addresses descriptively but does not test.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW

Three things, in descending order of how well the design supports them. First, the advanced-coursework result. The claim that EL classification restricts access to rigorous coursework has been asserted descriptively for two decades (Callahan 2005; Callahan et al. 2010; Kanno & Kangas 2014), and the three RD studies that tested it found nothing (p. 5). This paper finds a robust positive effect of exiting EL status on earning advanced credit — 3.1 pp ITT on a 10.1% base, 7.5 pp CATE, with subject-specific effects in English (+5.4 pp CATE on a 4.2% base) and social studies (+6.2 pp on a 6.9% base) and true nulls in math and science (Table 2, p. 13). The math/science nulls are informative, not a failure: they fit a story in which the constraint operates through ELA/humanities scheduling and gatekeeping rather than general tracking, which is what the ELD-crowd-out literature would predict. This is the paper's real contribution to knowledge.

Second, the design. Conditioning on all three TELPAS domains and then using STAAR as the running variable is a genuine improvement over binding-score RDs, which cannot say which criterion produces the effect. The authors state the counterfactual crisply on p. 10: "if Texas did not include the state ELA content exam as part of the reclassification process, all students in our analytic sample would be eligible to reclassify based on TELPAS performance." That is a well-posed policy question, and the 39-point first stage (Figure 1, p. 11) means the design has real bite.

Third, the setting. Texas is the highest-EL-share state and had no comparable causal evidence. The decentralized LPAC structure, the five-EOC graduation requirement, and the elementary bilingual-instruction mandate (pp. 5–6) genuinely distinguish Texas from California and Wisconsin, and the paper argues plausibly for transferability to Florida.

WHAT IS LESS NEW

The negative-outcomes half largely reproduces the LAUSD pattern (Robinson-Cimpian & Thompson 2016; Betts et al. 2020): lenient exit criteria produce worse high school outcomes; tightening criteria eliminates the harm. Texas has already tightened, adding the ELP reading exam (p. 20). So the policy configuration studied here is historical. That is a normal fate for reclassification research and does not void the evidence, but it does mean the paper is better read as "the LAUSD result generalizes to a very different statewide context" than as a new discovery.

THE ESTIMAND AND HOW FAR IT TRAVELS

Precisely stated, the CATE is: for eighth-grade ML-ELs in Texas who met all three TELPAS oral/writing thresholds, failed the first STAAR Reading administration, retook it, and scored within about 5 raw points of the cutoff, the effect of being reclassified rather than remaining EL-classified and receiving state-mandated accelerated reading instruction. Three restrictions each shrink the reach. The TELPAS restriction defines a high-oral-proficiency population (32% of ML-ELs). The second-administration restriction selects on prior academic failure — Table A2 confirms these students are lower-performing than first-attempt takers, and Table 1 (p. 8) shows 16% met the Grade 7 Reading standard versus 31% among all ML-ELs. The bandwidth restriction is standard RD locality. The authors defend the resulting population well (p. 19): the high-oral/low-literacy profile is characteristic of long-term ML-ELs, and every state that mandates ELA for reclassification allows retakes, so the retake margin exists elsewhere. That defense is convincing on relevance but does not extend the estimate to ML-ELs generally.

The harder limit is the substitute-versus-additional problem. Because Texas replaced ELP reading with STAAR rather than adding it, the paper cannot answer the question its title asks about the current policy landscape. Adding a criterion mechanically makes exit harder; substituting a lenient criterion for a stringent one makes exit easier. Texas's own numbers make this vivid: 44% of eighth-grade ML-ELs passed STAAR Reading on the first try versus 24% meeting "advanced high" on TELPAS reading (p. 6). So the treatment studied is closer to loosening than to tightening. The authors see this clearly (p. 20: "difficult to disentangle whether the negative effects ... are driven by the content assessed on the ELA exam or by the lower passing standard"), but the paper's positioning — "some of the first state-level evidence on the effects of using academic reclassification criteria" (p. 2) — will be cited past that boundary.

THE EXCLUSION-RESTRICTION PROBLEM

This deserves more weight than the paper gives it. The STAAR cutoff is not only the reclassification threshold; it is the exam's own passing threshold, and repeated failure triggers accelerated instruction and possible retention (p. 11; footnote 6, p. 22). The authors state the implication plainly on p. 2 — the counterfactual is "remaining EL and accessing additional academic support" — and then, in the discussion (p. 18), actually invoke that support as an explanation for the negative results. But once the extra reading support is a live mechanism, the estimate is no longer the effect of reclassification; it is the effect of a bundle, and the bundle's academic-support component may be doing much of the work in the achievement and graduation findings. The paper does not attempt to unbundle it, even though footnote 6 notes districts varied substantially in delivery, which is exactly the variation a heterogeneity test could exploit. This is the single most important thing for a reader to hold in mind, and the reason the graduation numbers should be treated as an upper bound.

QUOTABLE VERSUS SUPPORTED

The abstract's line — "Reclassified students earn more advanced credits, but graduate high school at lower rates" — is the sentence that will be quoted. Its two halves have very different evidentiary standing. The first half is the paper's cleanest, most novel, best-replicated result. The second half is large, statistically significant, and stable across specifications, but it rests on a comparison whose control condition includes an academic intervention, and its magnitude (−10.1 pp CATE on on-time graduation off an 83.3% base) is at the far end of what the literature reports. The abstract's policy prescription — "increased support for former ML-ELs" — is one of two readings the evidence permits; the other, "the exit bar was too low," is arguably better supported by the paper's own numbers and is the conclusion Texas itself acted on. The paper acknowledges this on p. 20 but does not carry the acknowledgment into the abstract.

STANDING AND OPEN QUESTIONS

On eighth-grade reclassification effects in Texas, this is now the best available evidence and will remain so for some time; state administrative data of this scope is not easily replicated. On the general question of whether states should use academic criteria, it is a useful but partial input, and the field should resist treating it as settling that debate. The paper itself names the right next study (p. 20): explicitly test the effect of requiring both ELP and ELA, which is what most large ML-EL states now do. Two further gaps are worth naming: postsecondary outcomes, which is where the advanced-credit gain would show its value and where Carlson & Knowles found their strongest effects; and a mechanism design that separates the loss of EL services from the loss of accelerated instruction. The suggestive ESL-program and school-EL-share splits (p. 18) point in a plausible direction — that comprehensive EL services are doing real work and their abrupt withdrawal is costly — but they are explicitly underpowered and the authors concede the pattern is consistent with opposite interpretations. Readers should treat that as an agenda item, not a result.

One last note in the paper's favor: the internal tension between more advanced credits and more course failures is the kind of finding many authors would bury. Confronting it in footnote 7 (p. 22), and reporting that about 70% of advanced-course takers do not fail a core humanities course, is the right instinct — it says the two effects operate on distinct subgroups, which is both more honest and more interesting than a clean single-direction story would have been. It also implies the real policy question is heterogeneity: which marginal ML-ELs benefit from exit and which are harmed. The paper poses that question well without answering it, and that is a reasonable thing for a paper to leave the field.

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper names its data source and steward (Texas Education Agency via the University of Houston Education Research Center, p. 21) and its estimation software (rdrobust in Stata, p. 11), and it reports coefficients, clustered standard errors, control means, per-outcome sample sizes, and an unusually full set of diagnostics — but every diagnostic lives in an online supplement, and the article carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no software version information. More consequentially for verification, several load-bearing details of the design are internally inconsistent or unstated: the reported bandwidth appears as 5, 5.36, and 5.25 points in three places; the running variable is described as recentered raw scores in the text but "standardized raw scores" in a footnote; and a sample exclusion (students who received linguistic accommodations) appears only in a table note. An authorized ERC replicator could get close to these results, but not without guessing on choices that move the estimates.

**Strengths:**

- The data source and its access channel are identifiable: the Acknowledgments (p. 21) name the Texas Education Agency and the University of Houston Education Research Center as the data provider, which points a would-be replicator at a real, documented restricted-use application pathway even though the paper never spells out the application process, data-use agreement, or a project/IRB number.
- The estimation machinery is named with citations rather than described vaguely: local polynomial nonparametric regression via the rdrobust Stata package (Calonico et al., 2017), CCT bandwidth selection (Calonico et al., 2014), triangular kernel, local linear polynomial, and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors clustered at the eighth-grade school level (p. 11). Density/manipulation testing is tied to Cattaneo et al. (2018), i.e., rddensity. A replicator therefore knows which estimator to call, if not exactly how it was called.
- The sample-construction logic is laid out as an explicit ordered list of five restrictions (p. 7) — EL-classified in eighth grade, valid TELPAS and STAAR Reading scores, "advanced high" on TELPAS speaking/listening/writing, took the second STAAR administration, re-enrolled in a Texas public school in ninth grade — with the analytic N (21,044) reported and a rationale given for each restriction. Table 1 then benchmarks the analytic sample against all eighth-grade ML-ELs (208,060), so a replicator can check whether their reconstructed sample looks right before estimating anything.
- Cohort coverage and the outcome window are unambiguous: five eighth-grade cohorts, 2012–13 through 2016–17, followed through spring 2022 (pp. 7, 9).
- The diagnostic suite a reader would want is actually run and pointed to: covariate balance (Table A4), a density plot and year-by-year manipulation tests (Figure B2, Table A5), bandwidth sensitivity from 4 to 10 points (Tables A6–A9), placebo cutoffs shifted ±4 points (Tables A10–A13), exclusion of the COVID-affected 2016 and 2017 cohorts (Tables A14–A17), and three separate attrition checks including a common-sample re-estimation and a ninth-grade non-enrollment test (Tables A18–A26) (pp. 11, 16–17). Notably, the paper reports that the negative Algebra I effect loses significance under the common-sample restriction (p. 17) rather than burying it.
- Uncertainty is reported throughout: every estimate in Tables 2–5 carries a standard error, a control mean in brackets, and an outcome-specific N, and Table 3's note explains why Ns vary across EOC exams. Nothing central is reported as a bare point estimate.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement anywhere in the article, and no replication or code package — not deposited, not promised, not even "available upon request." For a 2026 EEPA article this is a norm gap, not merely an inconvenience: nothing tells a reader how to apply for the ERC data, what the approval timeline or cost is, or whether the authors will share do-files with an approved replicator.
- The bandwidth cannot be pinned down from the paper. Page 11 states the main results use "the optimal bandwidth from the first stage estimation (Equation 2; Bandwidth (BW) = 5 points) for all of our main results," but the notes to Tables 2, 4, and 5 report BW = 5.36 points and the note to Table 3 reports BW = 5.25 points. Three different numbers, and no explanation for why the achievement tables use a different bandwidth than the course-taking and graduation tables despite the text's claim of a single first-stage bandwidth. A replicator matching to two decimal places has to guess which is right.
- The running variable's construction is ambiguous. The Measures section (p. 7) and Equation 1 (p. 10) describe raw STAAR Reading scores "recentered so that 0 is the passing score," and bandwidths are expressed in "points," which reads as raw points. But footnote 5 (p. 22) says "we chose to use standardized raw scores," and Table 1 defines the analytic sample as "within 2 SDs around the passing cutoff" (p. 8). Raw-recentered and standardized are different variables producing different bandwidths and different samples. Compounding this, the raw scale changed across years (0–52, but 0–44 in 2016–17, p. 7), so pooling cohorts requires a rescaling decision the paper never states — cohort fixed effects absorb level differences but not differences in the metric of the running variable.
- The year-specific passing cutoffs are not tabulated. Footnote 5 gives only 2015 (scale 1,575 = raw 27) and 2017 (scale 1,587 = raw 24), and directs readers to TEA conversion tables that are "publicly available on the Texas Education Agency website" without a URL, table name, or retrieval date. Three of five cohorts' raw cutoffs are simply absent, and the 2016–17 standard changed name ("Approaches standard"). Since the cutoff defines treatment, every one of these has to be recovered by hand from archived TEA documents.
- A sample restriction appears only in a table note and contradicts the main text. Main-text restriction (d) is "took the second administration of STAAR" (p. 7); the Table 1 note (p. 8) instead reads "failed the first STAAR attempt and re-took the second administration without receiving linguistic accommodations." The accommodations exclusion is never mentioned, motivated, or quantified in the text, and "took the second administration" and "failed the first attempt" are not the same condition. Whether 21,044 is the pre- or post-2SD-trim count is also unclear — Table 1's column header says "within 2 SD" while the text calls 21,044 the "final analytic sample."
- The treatment variable for the fuzzy stage is defined conceptually but not operationally. The paper says reclassification is an LPAC decision and that the study effectively measures "entering high school classified as English proficient rather than as an EL" (pp. 8–9), but never states which administrative field or flag encodes this — ninth-grade EL status indicator, a reclassification/exit date, a monitored-former-EL code — or how mid-year status changes are handled. In Texas administrative files these are distinct variables that do not coincide.
- Outcome construction is under-specified for a replicator working in raw Texas course files. "Advanced" credit is AP, IB, or dual enrollment, and remedial courses are "Math Models," "Strategies for High School Math," and "Integrated Physics and Chemistry" (p. 9) — but no PEIMS/TEA service-ID course-code lists are given, and course-code crosswalks are exactly where independent replications diverge. Similarly, "ever failing a course" in a core subject is never defined in terms of an underlying variable, which sits awkwardly with the paper's own statement that grades are unavailable ("a rough proxy for student grades, which we do not have access to," p. 9); how EOC scores were standardized (statewide by year? within the analytic sample?) is not stated; and "officially dropping out" presumably maps to a specific leaver code that is not named.
- The covariate vector is described with "such as" rather than enumerated: "student demographics, achievement in seventh grade, and number of years enrolled in high school; eighth-grade school covariates, such as demographics and average achievement; and dummy variables for school region" (p. 10). "School region" is undefined (ESC region? district region? Table notes say "district region"). Since Columns 2 and 4 are the preferred specifications, the preferred models cannot be re-run from the description alone. Separately, "number of years enrolled in high school" is plausibly post-treatment, which is a specification concern as well as a transparency one.
- No first-stage statistics are reported. The 39-percentage-point jump is given in the text and Figure 1 note (p. 11) with no standard error, no F-statistic or effective-sample diagnostic, and no table. Every CATE in Tables 2–5 is scaled by this first stage, so its precision is load-bearing and is nowhere shown.
- No software environment is documented beyond the package name: no Stata version, no rdrobust version (rdrobust's default variance estimator and bandwidth behavior changed materially across releases, so this affects exact replication), no statement of whether rdrobust's conventional or robust bias-corrected estimates are the ones tabulated, and no indication of how covariates and cohort fixed effects were passed to rdrobust. There is also no preregistration and no IRB or data-use-agreement statement.
- Essentially all verification material — every balance test, density test, placebo, bandwidth sweep, attrition check, and the two mechanism analyses that carry much of the Discussion's interpretive weight (Tables A27–A35) — sits in an online supplement not contained in the article. The paper's claim that results are "robust to different model specifications and bandwidths" (p. 2) is, from the article alone, taken entirely on trust.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the article's headline estimates as reproducible in direction but not to the digit. Before citing a specific magnitude, note that the paper reports three different bandwidths (5 in text on p. 11; 5.36 in Tables 2, 4, 5; 5.25 in Table 3) and two different descriptions of the running variable (recentered raw points, pp. 7 and 10, versus "standardized raw scores," footnote 5, p. 22). Any exact re-estimation should ask the authors which combination generated the tables.
- If you are pursuing a replication, the access pathway is a restricted-use application to the University of Houston Education Research Center for TEA data (Acknowledgments, p. 21) — not the UT-Austin ERC. Budget for the application and approval process, and request from the authors, at minimum: the do-files, the year-by-year raw-score cutoffs for all five cohorts, the course-code lists behind the AP/IB/DE and remedial-course indicators, and the exact administrative field used to code reclassification. None of these can be recovered from the article.
- Rebuild the sample cautiously: the main text and the Table 1 note give different restrictions (p. 7 says "took the second administration"; the Table 1 note on p. 8 adds "failed the first STAAR attempt" and "without receiving linguistic accommodations"). The accommodations exclusion is undocumented and could plausibly shift the composition of the marginal sample, since accommodation use is correlated with the ELP and academic profile that defines this study's population. Check how sensitive the estimates are to including accommodated retakers.
- The CATE estimates in Columns 3 and 4 of every table are the ITT scaled by a first stage whose precision is never reported (the 39-percentage-point jump appears only in the Figure 1 note, p. 11, without a standard error or F-statistic). Lean on the ITT estimates, which are directly estimated and fully reported, when you need a number you can check.
- The Discussion's mechanism story — that negative effects concentrate in ESL All Content schools and in schools with larger ML-EL populations (p. 18) — rests entirely on Supplemental Tables A27–A34, which are not in the article and which the authors themselves describe as imprecise and "not significant at conventional levels." Retrieve the supplement before repeating those subgroup patterns, and treat them as exploratory regardless.
- Verify the robustness claims yourself rather than accepting the summary. The bandwidth sweep (A6–A9), placebo cutoffs (A10–A13), COVID-cohort exclusion (A14–A17), and attrition tests (A18–A26) are all offloaded to the online supplement. Note in particular the authors' own disclosure (p. 17) that the negative Algebra I EOC effect loses statistical significance when all outcomes are estimated on a common sample — that is the one main-text result the paper flags as fragile, and it is the achievement result most often paired with the graduation finding in the abstract's narrative.
- The advanced-coursework and graduation results are the paper's two headline claims, and they are reported with full standard errors, control means, and Ns, so their internal consistency is checkable from the tables as printed. What is not checkable from the article alone is the mapping from Texas administrative files to those variables — so treat the effect sizes as well-reported and the variable definitions as the place where an independent replication would most likely diverge.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a restricted-data administrative study, so the absence of a public dataset is not itself a mark against it — the question is whether the article documents enough for an approved ERC replicator to rebuild the analysis and for an ordinary reader to know what is being taken on trust. On the second question the paper does reasonably well; on the first it falls short in specific, identifiable places.

WHAT IS DOCUMENTED WELL

The design description is unusually clear about the logic of the frontier RD: condition on "advanced high" TELPAS performance in speaking, listening, and writing (p. 10), then exploit the STAAR Reading passing threshold as the sole remaining test-based criterion, with the explicit observation that absent the ELA criterion every student in the sample would already be reclassification-eligible. The estimator is named with citations (rdrobust; CCT bandwidth selection; triangular kernel; local linear; SEs clustered at the eighth-grade school), the estimands (ITT and CATE) are distinguished and separately motivated (p. 12), and the cohort window and follow-up horizon are stated. The reporting discipline in Tables 2–5 is good: standard errors, control means, and outcome-specific Ns throughout, with the note to Table 3 explaining why Ns move across EOC exams. The paper also volunteers a result that cuts against it — that the Algebra I effect does not survive the common-sample attrition check (p. 17).

WHERE A REPLICATOR HAS TO GUESS

There are six distinct places, and they compound. First, the bandwidth: the text says 5 points and says a single first-stage bandwidth governs all main results (p. 11), while the tables report 5.36 (Tables 2, 4, 5) and 5.25 (Table 3). Second, the running variable: recentered raw points (pp. 7, 10) versus "standardized raw scores" (footnote 5, p. 22), with Table 1 additionally defining the sample as "within 2 SDs" of the cutoff. These are different objects and cannot both be right; the choice determines the sample and the bandwidth's meaning. Third, the year-specific cutoffs: only 2015 and 2017 appear anywhere, and the TEA conversion tables are cited without a URL or table identifier. Fourth, the sample restrictions: the accommodations exclusion appears only in the Table 1 note and is never motivated. Fifth, the reclassification flag: the paper describes an LPAC decision but never names the administrative variable that operationalizes it, and in Texas files the candidates (ninth-grade EL indicator, exit date, monitored-former-EL code) are not interchangeable. Sixth, outcome construction: no course-code lists for AP/IB/DE or the named remedial courses, no definition of "ever failing a core course" against an underlying field, and no statement of the standardization metric for EOC scores.

Any one of these would be an ordinary documentation gap. Together they mean that an approved replicator working from the article alone would produce a different analytic sample, a different running variable, and a different bandwidth than the authors did — and would have no way to tell whether a discrepancy in results reflected a coding error or a different guess. That is what pushes this below "adequate" despite the paper's genuinely strong diagnostic effort.

THE SUPPLEMENT PROBLEM

The article's robustness claims are extensive and almost entirely external to the article: at least 35 appendix tables and two appendix figures are referenced. That is commendable work, but it means the reviewed artifact contains none of the evidence for the claim that results are "robust to different model specifications and bandwidths" (p. 2). Readers who do not retrieve the supplement are accepting the entire identification-check apparatus — balance, manipulation, placebo, attrition — on the authors' summary of it. The two mechanism analyses (ESL program type; ML-EL school share) are in the same position and carry substantial weight in the Discussion despite being described by the authors as imprecise.

JOURNAL-ERA EXPECTATIONS

EEPA published this in 2026 with a Declaration of Conflicting Interests and a Funding statement (p. 21) but no data availability statement and no open-practices badge or equivalent. Given that the data are restricted, no one should expect a public deposit — but a statement naming the UH ERC application process, and a deposited code package usable by any researcher who obtains the same data, are both entirely feasible under a restricted-use agreement and are increasingly standard. Neither is present, and the paper does not offer code even conditionally. That absence, combined with no reported Stata or rdrobust version and no statement of whether the tabulated estimates are rdrobust's conventional or robust bias-corrected output, means the exact numbers in Tables 2–5 are not independently checkable by anyone.

BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS

The substantive findings — positive effects on advanced course credit, negative effects on graduation and on-time graduation — are reported with enough uncertainty information to be evaluated as evidence, and the qualitative pattern is unlikely to hinge on the ambiguities above. The precise magnitudes are a different matter: they depend on a bandwidth the paper reports inconsistently, a running variable it describes two ways, and a sample defined partly in a table note. Cite the direction and the approximate size with confidence; cite the second decimal place only after corresponding with the authors.
